newsitem.title: bosnia: Bosnian post-war elections results confirmed.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian post-war elections results confirmed.

text.p: The international body supervising Bosnia's first post-war elections announced on Sunday it had certified the results of national balloting which took place on September 14th.

"I think it was a reasonably democratic process and a reasonably democratic result which reflects the will of the people," Ambassador Robert Frowick, head of the OSCE mission in Bosnia, told reporters in Sarajevo.
The OSCE (Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe) received its mandate in Bosnia through the Dayton peace agreement, which brought an end to 43-months of war in December 1995.

Sunday's decision by the OSCE's Provisional Election Commission ended days of haggling over voting irregularities and cleared the way for formation of new government institutions envisioned under the Dayton agreement.
Frowick rejected allegations of fraud in the result but declined to characterise the September 14 elections as "free and fair" even though that was the requirement set forth in the Dayton accord.
He said it was inappropriate to judge the balloting according to such a strict Western standard because of the complex situation prevailing in post-war Bosnia.

The Dayton pact called for freedom of movement, freedom of the press, the right of refugees to return to their homes and a neutral political environment as conditions for the elections. Frowick said those conditions were only partially met.

The final lifting of sanctions against rump Yugoslavia and Bosnia's Serb republic, imposed as a result of their role in the war, depends in part upon whether U.N. Security Council members believe the elections satisfied Dayton's requirements.

The certfied results give Bosnia a new three-man national Presidency, a national House of Representatives, separate Moslem-Croat and Serb parliaments, a Serb republic President and 10 cantonal assemblies.
Alija Izetbegovic, who led Bosnian Moslems through the war, won the most votes in a contest for the collective presidency and will serve as that body's chairman for the next two years.
Diplomats have been working behind the scenes to schedule a first meeting of the Moslem, Serb and Croat members of the presidency but the date and place are proving a problem.
Izetbegovic and Kresimir Zubak, the Croat member, were willing to meet in Moslem-Croat controlled Sarajevo as soon as Monday, September 30. The Serb member, Momcilo Krajisnik, expressed reservations.
At one point Krajisnik suggested a new building on the dividing line between Bosnia's Serb republic and its Moslem- Croat federation, with a door on Serb territory through which he could enter.
Such manoeuvring is a preview of the problems most analysts expect the new institutions to encounter in conducting business.
